title: Jacob Spears & early "Bourbon" whiskey

bodyMarkdown:
Jacob Spears was one of the early distillers who helped give Bourbon County's whiskey its reputation. [ExploreKYHistory](https://explorekyhistory.ky.gov/items/show/427) gives his dates as 1754 to about 1825 and describes a man of several trades. He was a farmer, a distiller, a dealer in bluegrass seed and a breeder of fine horses.

## Stone Castle

The [Kentucky Historical Society marker on bourbon whiskey and Jacob Spears](https://history.ky.gov/markers/bourbon-whiskey-jacob-spears) calls him a Pennsylvanian who settled in Paris and "one of first distillers of bourbon whiskey." It says Thomas Metcalfe built Stone Castle for Spears in 1790.

The farm still has a springhouse and a storehouse for Spears's whiskey. The marker calls it "the most complete distiller's complex still in existence today." The marker was dedicated on June 28, 2009.

## A county full of stills

Spears was not unusual in his trade. ExploreKYHistory says the 1810 census of Bourbon County counted 128 distilleries, which made more than 146,000 gallons of whiskey worth over $48,000. Every community in the county had at least one large distillery.

ExploreKYHistory explains that corn was the major ingredient. It was combined with wheat, barley or rye and with water from local limestone springs. [ExploreKYHistory's article on Bourbon County whiskey](https://explorekyhistory.ky.gov/items/show/418) notes that one early notice in the Paris *Western Citizen* offered "Bourbon whiskey by the barrel or keg." Spears and his partner Samuel Williams sold their own brand as "Best Old Whiskey."

## Down the rivers

Getting whiskey to market meant using the rivers. According to the [Hopewell Museum in Paris](https://www.hopewellmuseum.org/learn/historic-preservation/bourbon-county-historical-markers/bourbon-whiskey-jacob-spears/), two of Spears's three sons, Abraham and Noah, are said to have loaded barrels onto flatboats on Cooper's Run. From there the boats went down the Licking River to the Ohio and Mississippi and on to New Orleans, where they sold the "Old Bourbon" for a good price.

The museum presents this as a family tradition ("are said to have"). Other historians have suggested different routes for Bourbon County whiskey, so the exact path is uncertain.

## What "bourbon" came to mean

By the middle of the 1800s, bourbon was a nationally recognized type of whiskey, according to ExploreKYHistory. The KHS marker explains the modern definition. Bourbon is made from a fermented mash of at least 51 percent corn, distilled at no more than 160 proof and aged in charred oak barrels.

In 1964 Congress recognized bourbon as a distinctly American product. For more on the spirit, see [Grokipedia's article on bourbon whiskey](https://grokipedia.com/page/Bourbon_whiskey).

Who first used the name "bourbon" is still debated, and no source checked here credits Spears alone. The marker places him among the first distillers of bourbon, not as its inventor.

## Kentucky today

The KHS marker stands at the crossroads of Clay-Kiser Road and US 27 in Paris. Stone Castle is about a mile to the south on private land. Paris itself was first chartered as Hopewell; see [Paris from Hopewell](/stories/paris-from-hopewell/).
